technique: scale — moving between the tiny and the large in a few lines
poem:
A crow starts it, one rasp off the ridge,
then nothing, then the cold goes about its business.
You hear the boards answer your own weight,
each one a number you've learned to trust,
the way you've learned the tally of a week —
hours and dollars squared to the last cent,
the small accounting that keeps a place upright.
Coffee cooling. The window holds a field
gone rust and ash, the maples burning down
to their honest wood. There's a debt you'd rather
settle clean than argue, and a measure of red
sitting sealed on the sill, patient as you are.

There's a fresh coat waiting to go on, and your hands know the brush better than anyone's.

So — up!
lesson: Today, we work on one thing, scale. Scale means the poem moves between something small and something large in just a few lines, so you feel the size of each by putting them next to each other. Here is where this poem does it. It starts tiny, one rasp off the ridge. Then it pulls back to a whole season, a field gone rust and ash, the maples burning down. Then it shrinks again to one small object, a measure of red sitting sealed on the sill. This works in a plain way. When you jump from the small thing to the big thing, the small thing feels larger and the big thing feels close enough to touch. The crow and the can of paint matter more because the hills sit next to them. Try this. Put one small object in a line, then in the next line name something much bigger and let them sit together without explaining the jump. The second time through, listen for how the small sealed paint leads into the last line, so up.
